title: What Dad Said

pages.text:
*Rule 15 of the Library at the Bottom of the Sea: Slow readers read deepest.*

The sea wall was cold and wet under her boots. Wren scrambled up the rocks, slipping once, her yellow soles squeaking against the slick stone. Her eyes stung. The salt air hit her face, sharp and clean, but she could not breathe properly.

Ben Tidewell sat on the edge of the wall, his legs dangling over the water. He held a thermos in one hand and a small, warm cup in the other. He did not look surprised to see her. He just looked tired, and sad, and ready.

"Hi, Wren-bird," he said. His voice was low and steady, like the water lapping at the rocks below.

"I didn't go far," he added, turning to face her. "I just waited. I saw the light on the water. It looked... worried."

Wren slid down beside him. Her knees knocked together. She wanted to cry, but her throat felt tight, as if a knot had formed there and refused to loosen. She looked at the horizon, where the dark blue sea met the darker sky.

"Dad," she whispered.

"I'm here," he said. He passed her the cup. It was tea, hot and sweet, with a slice of lemon floating in it.

She took it. The warmth seeped into her palms, pushing back the chill that had settled in her bones.
pages.image: Wren sits on a wet stone sea wall next to Ben, who holds a steaming thermos, with dark water lapping at the rocks below.

pages.text:
Wren drank the tea. It tasted like home, and like safety, and it made her stomach ache less. She told him about the words. Not just the ones that swam, but the ones that ran away, the ones that hid in the corners of the page, and the ones that whispered she was slow.

She told him about the stomachaches, the lies, and the quiet in Room 4 that felt heavier than any wave. And then, because he was her dad and he had the thermos and the patience of a stone, she told him about the door in the sea wall. She told him about the octopus with the pince-nez, the fish that glowed only when you read to them, and the crab who said she was useless.

Ben listened. He did not ask questions. He did not fix it. He just watched the gulls wheeling above the harbor, their wings beating the air in slow, sure circles.

"I'm not any use," Wren said, and the words came out smaller than she wanted them to.

Ben nodded. He looked at the gulls, and then at her. "Tell me about the crab," he said. "What did he say, exactly?"

"He said I can't save them. He said I'm too slow. He said the books are turning to sand because I'm useless."
pages.image: Wren sits on a dock bench holding a small cup, looking down, while her dad Ben sits beside her watching seagulls circle over the harbor.

pages.text:
Ben reached into his navy sweater and pulled out a thick, leather-bound book, the ship's log for the *Gull*, its cover worn smooth and its edges frayed from years of salt and use.

"Look," he said, opening it to a recent entry.

The words were cramped and slanted, written in ink that had faded to a soft, tea-stained brown. Ben did not just look at them. He placed his index finger under the first line, then the second, moving it slowly and deliberately to track each word as if he were counting steps in the dark.

"I was the slowest reader in my class, Wren-bird," he said, his finger stopping on the date. "I still am. I learned the tide tables as rhymes because it was quicker than reading the columns. I still do it that way."

Wren stared at his finger. It was steady and strong, and it was not hiding.

"You read with a finger?" she asked.

"Sometimes," he said. "It helps the words stay still. Just like yours, maybe, if you find the right way to hold them."

He closed the book. "I didn't tell you. I was afraid you'd think I was broken."

"I didn't think you were broken," Wren said. "I thought you were magic."
pages.image: A close-up of a man's hand with a finger tracing a line of text in a worn leather book held by a girl with deep-brown skin, their faces out of frame, with a blurred background of water and sky.

pages.text:
Ben leaned back against the stone, the roughness pressing through his navy sweater. He looked at Wren, and his face held an expression she had not expected. It was not pity, and it was not surprise. It was a deep, quiet pride, settled in him like sand on the sea floor.

"Slow readers see everything," he said. "Fast readers skim. They miss the texture. They miss the weight. Slow readers stay with each word. They let it sink in."

He gestured to the dark water beyond the wall. "That is why you remember every story. You do not just listen. You live inside it. You let it breathe."

Wren blinked. The tight knot in her throat loosened, just a little.

"So I am not useless?" she asked.

"No," he said. "You are thorough. That is a very different thing. And much more useful, if you ask me. Useless people do not notice when the light changes color."

Wren looked at the sea. The faint pulse of the lantern below was still visible in the dark. She thought of the Glimmers, silent and dim, and the books slowly turning to sand.

She took a breath. It felt easier than the last one.
pages.image: Ben leans against a stone wall, gesturing toward the dark water, while Wren looks up at him with wide eyes.

pages.text:
Wren leaned her head against his shoulder. His sweater smelled of salt and diesel and warm wool, a scent that felt as safe as the bottom of a sleeping bag.

A small, rusty laugh came out of her, like a gate hinge that had been stuck for a whole summer.

"I'm going back down," she said.

Ben didn't look surprised. He just nodded, his beard brushing her hair. "Of course you are."

"I'm going to bring the truth. Not just the book. Me. The slow me. The me who stumbles."

Ben put his arm around her shoulders, pulling her close. Behind them, the ferry *Gull* rocked gently in the harbor, creaking its wooden joints in the dark. Above, the lighthouse beam swept across the sky, white and slow and patient, searching for something that wasn't lost, only waiting.

Wren closed her eyes. She didn't need to see the words right now. She just needed to know they were there, holding still, ready for her.

"Right," she said. "One page."
pages.image: A girl with short black curls in a coral-red sweater leans her head on the shoulder of a man in a navy sweater, both sitting on a stone wall at night, with a bright white lighthouse beam sweeping across the dark sky above the water.
